Collision Report — i2m Futures Innovation

From Industrial Scrap to Cross-Industry Value

Different perspectives challenge one cross-industry materials idea.

MANN+HUMMEL · 12 October 2026 · V3.4
Fixed challenge

How might we build a fully integrated reverse logistics system that returns industrial scrap and waste to a central hub, then redirects usable materials across sectors—for example, textile offcuts becoming inputs for acoustic products?

DISCLAIMER

This website contains AI-generated content created for demonstration purposes. The viewpoints, ideas, analyses, and dialogue presented are fictional illustrations and do not represent actual statements, beliefs, or positions of any referenced individual or of MANN+HUMMEL. Content is provided solely for illustrative purposes and should not be considered factual information or used as the basis for business or strategic decisions.

Step 01 / 05

Challenge Framing

The material-flow challenge, current losses and desired gains.

Job-to-be-Done

When manufacturers generate usable scrap or need secondary materials, they want a reliable way to return, qualify and redirect those materials across sectors, so they can reduce disposal, secure useful inputs and capture value without disrupting production.

Top 3 Pains
  • Usable industrial scrap is discarded because its quality, location or next use is unclear.
  • Cross-sector transfers face uncertain specifications, ownership and logistics costs.
  • Suppliers and buyers lack a trusted way to prove material origin and performance.
Top 3 Gains
  • Verified matches between available scrap and suitable industrial applications.
  • Lower disposal and virgin-material demand where quality and economics permit.
  • Traceable material flows and a repeatable business model for participants.
Step 02 / 05

Expert Panel

Distinct perspectives selected to challenge the concept.

The panel examines material circularity through systems design, measurable environmental impact, practical economics, logistics scale, market incentives and inclusive governance. These are simulated analytical lenses, not the named individuals’ stated views on this proposal.
Expert 01

Ani Dasgupta

H6 · President & CEO, World Resources Institute

Systems-oriented climate and development leader who views environmental action as inseparable from economic development, urban transformation, equity and human well-being. Connects local interventions to institutional scale, governance, finance, inclusion and implementation capacity.

Bold Idea

Design a multi-sector governance model for a shared material hub, with clear responsibilities for classification, traceability, financing and regional rollout.

Provocation

Who operates the hub, verifies material quality and makes the model work beyond one pilot?

Expert 02

Kate Orff

H7 · Landscape architect · Founder, SCAPE

Treats landscapes as active infrastructure and favors ecological, adaptive and place-specific solutions that protect people while restoring natural systems. Looks for hybrid blue-green infrastructure, biodiversity, community value and resilience rather than isolated hard-engineering fixes.

Bold Idea

Map material flows by place and design collection nodes that fit existing industrial clusters, transport routes and local environmental needs.

Provocation

Does centralizing every material improve the whole regional system, or create unnecessary transport and handling?

Expert 03

Greta Thunberg

H8 · Climate activist · Fridays for Future

Evaluates proposals through measurable climate impact, ecological limits and intergenerational responsibility rather than corporate narratives or incremental improvement. Looks for real emissions reduction, speed, scientific alignment and evidence of greenwashing or delayed action.

Bold Idea

Set a life-cycle impact threshold for every proposed material exchange, including collection, sorting, transport and avoided virgin production.

Provocation

Which transfers produce a real net environmental benefit rather than a circularity label?

Expert 04

William McDonough

H9 · Architect · Cradle-to-Cradle pioneer

Moves beyond “less bad” sustainability toward regenerative systems where materials are designed for continuous biological or technical cycles. Treats waste, toxicity and disposability as design failures and asks what every material becomes next.

Bold Idea

Create material passports and design specifications that make textile offcuts and other secondary streams safe, useful inputs for their next application.

Provocation

Can the material enter a high-value next cycle without contamination or downcycling by default?

Expert 05

Julian Simon

H10 · Economist · Counter-Malthusian thinker

Views human ingenuity, knowledge, markets and technological substitution as the ultimate resource capable of turning scarcity into innovation and abundance. Looks for price signals, entrepreneurship, substitution, discovery and unintended consequences of restricting growth.

Bold Idea

Use a transparent cross-industry marketplace so demand, price and technical substitution reveal the best destinations for each scrap stream.

Provocation

Would open matching identify better uses than assigning every material to a predetermined central outlet?

Expert 06

Diana Furchtgott-Roth

H11 · Economist · Free-market policy advocate

Starts from affordability, reliability, resilience and economic competitiveness and is skeptical of mandates that impose large costs without demonstrated benefits. Stress-tests full economic cost, energy prices, industrial competitiveness, consumer choice and dependence on subsidies or regulation.

Bold Idea

Test a voluntary service model with visible collection, processing, transport and quality-assurance costs before proposing scale.

Provocation

Will suppliers and buyers choose this route when total cost, reliability and liability are clear?

Expert 07

Michael Shellenberger

H12 · Author · Environmental commentator

Combines environmental concern with advocacy for nuclear power, energy abundance, technological modernization and economic development. Looks for energy density, reliability, scalability and human welfare while challenging symbolic or high-cost climate policies.

Bold Idea

Concentrate collection and processing where material volumes justify the infrastructure; use direct transfers when a hub adds avoidable distance or energy.

Provocation

Does the reverse-logistics network move enough useful material to justify its physical footprint and energy use?

Expert 08

Wawa Gatheru

H13 · Founder & Executive Director, Black Girl Environmentalist

Climate solutions should be accessible and relevant to the communities they affect. Environmental action should include people historically underrepresented in climate leadership. Examines who helps design a solution, who benefits from it, who bears its costs, and whether affected communities have a meaningful role in decisions.

Bold Idea

Co-design the network with workers and communities near collection and processing sites, and include access to new roles and benefits in the pilot.

Provocation

Who helps shape the system, who receives the value, and who bears the local burden of sorting and transport?

Step 03 / 05

The Collision Meeting

Illustrative dialogue between the selected perspectives.

WM
William McDonough → responding to Julian Simon and Diana Furchtgott-Roth

A price is useful, but the exchange needs material identity and safe next-use specifications. Otherwise the network may simply move waste around.

JS
Julian Simon → responding to William McDonough and Kate Orff

Publish those specifications, then let buyers discover unexpected applications rather than assigning each stream to a single use.

GT
Greta Thunberg → responding to Michael Shellenberger and Diana Furchtgott-Roth

Compare the full route with disposal and virgin material. A transfer that adds more emissions than it avoids should not count as progress.

MS
Michael Shellenberger → responding to Greta Thunberg and Kate Orff

Agreed on measurement. A central hub should handle dense, repeatable flows; nearby direct exchanges may be more efficient for other materials.

KO
Kate Orff → responding to Michael Shellenberger and Ani Dasgupta

Choose collection points with the geography of industry and communities in mind, not only the neatness of a central diagram.

DF
Diana Furchtgott-Roth → responding to William McDonough and Greta Thunberg

Quality checks and emissions accounting have costs. Show suppliers and buyers the full economics before assuming they will join.

WG
Wawa Gatheru → responding to Kate Orff and Diana Furchtgott-Roth

The model also needs the perspectives of workers and nearby communities. Ask who handles the scrap, who gets paid and who lives with the traffic.

AD
Ani Dasgupta → responding to Wawa Gatheru and Julian Simon

Turn those tests into governance: shared standards, accountable operators and a way for multiple sectors to participate without losing local trust.

Step 04 / 05

Collision Combinations

Three ways to combine opposing lenses into a practical material network.

Combination

The Verified Material Exchange

Combine McDonough’s material passports with Simon’s open matching: qualifying scrap streams and allowing buyers in other sectors to identify valuable next uses.

Combination

Regional Hubs, Direct Routes

Combine Orff’s place-based systems lens with Shellenberger’s scale test: route high-volume streams through shared hubs and permit direct transfers where they perform better.

Combination

Circular Value With Shared Benefits

Combine Thunberg’s net-impact test, Furchtgott-Roth’s full-cost test and Gatheru’s inclusion lens: scale only exchanges that deliver measurable value without shifting burdens to workers or communities.

Step 05 / 05

The Final Concept

A cross-industry reverse-logistics concept and three first experiments.

Final Concept

Cross-Industry Material Loop

A proposed network that identifies usable industrial scrap, verifies material properties and routes it to suitable users in other sectors. A central source would coordinate standards and traceability, while regional hubs or direct transfers would be chosen according to volume, distance and economics. Textile offcuts supplied to acoustic-product makers are one test case, not a proven commercial application.

Why It Is Non-Obvious

The concept combines material qualification, matching, logistics and shared governance rather than assuming that any recovered stream has an immediate buyer. Its value depends on proving product suitability, total cost, net environmental benefit and fair participation together.

3 First Experiment Steps · ≤ 6 weeks
1

Map one textile offcut stream and interview at least one potential acoustic-product user; document volume, composition, current disposal route and the buyer’s technical acceptance criteria.

2

Run a small controlled transfer and material test; record sorting yield, transport distance, processing needs and whether the sample meets the buyer’s requirements.

3

Compare a central-hub route with a direct-transfer route using total cost, logistics effort and estimated life-cycle impact; define the threshold for a larger pilot with participating suppliers and buyers.
